Meta will buy environmental attribute certificates tied to 25 Nevoya battery-electric trucks on Interstate 10, a multi-year deal that gives the electric truckload carrier committed demand on a second freight lane. Nevoya, which announced the agreement Thursday, expects the Class 8 trucks to start running between San Bernardino, California, and Phoenix in 2027 and to cover about 4 million freight miles a year.
The deal is Meta’s second with Nevoya and the first it has signed on its own. In Texas, Meta was one of several buyers in the Center for Green Market Activation’s alliance, whose pooled certificate purchases support Nevoya’s 63-truck deployment between Houston and Dallas. The carrier, which raised a $9.3 million seed round in July 2025, said the I-10 agreement gives Meta a framework to add corridors in the future.
Meta’s purchase is not tied to hauling its own goods. Still, the release describes I-10 as a key route for moving data center construction materials across the southern United States. A FreightWaves SONAR analysis estimates data center construction will add 18.9 million truckloads nationwide from 2026 through 2031. Value chain emissions, known as scope 3, made up 99% of Meta’s 8.2 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024, according to its 2025 Sustainability Report .
“Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build,” Devon Lake, Meta’s head of net zero strategy, said in the release.
Deal terms and other tech buyers
Neither company disclosed the agreement’s value or length. Meta announced it Thursday in a newsroom post alongside purchases of low-carbon cement and near-zero-emission steel, part of a push to cut emissions in its data center supply chain . Meta has also backed zero-emission freight with NFI in Virginia, according to the post.
The Texas corridor reached 63 trucks after Google agreed in September to back 25 of them, a project Google said would cover about 11 million miles a year.
How the certificate purchase works
Under the agreement, Meta pays for the environmental attributes of Nevoya’s battery-electric freight service, issued as certificates, while the trucks haul freight for other shippers. Companies buy the certificates to address emissions across their value chains, including logistics, according to the release.
The approach is known as book and claim. Smart Freight Centre, a nonprofit that co-leads the Texas program with the Center for Green Market Activation, describes it as letting a low-emission shipment’s environmental attributes be “decoupled, traced, and accounted separately from the physical delivery,” in a December 2025 white paper on road freight.
In the Texas program, an independent, accredited auditor verifies the emissions impact as Nevoya operates the lane, CCJ reported in January. The release does not say who will verify the I-10 certificates.
Charging along the I-10 corridor
The deal includes bringing charging infrastructure online along the route, with the 25 trucks’ charging matched 100% with renewable energy certificates. Nevoya expects the chargers to be available to all freight operators on the corridor, and Meta described them as permanent, open-access stations. Neither company named a charging partner or sites.
Nevoya now has certificate buyers on two lanes. It first announced plans to run electric trucks on I-10 in August 2025.
“Meta coming back for a second corridor is a strong signal that this model works. Electric trucks already win on the corridors we run; what unlocks them at scale is multi-year demand that drives financial and operational innovation. That is what this agreement does, and we intend to repeat it corridor by corridor,” John Verdon, Nevoya’s co-founder and chief commercial officer, said in the release.
Why it matters: For fleets weighing electric trucks between the Inland Empire and Phoenix, the deal adds chargers Nevoya expects to open to every operator on I-10. Whether certificate money can sustain a fleet gets its first full test in early 2027, when the 63-truck Texas project is set to run.

( Stock image by Kaliel. )
Posted By: Mining.com Staff November 16, 2026
Two of China’s leading rare earth producers more than doubled their profits in the first nine months of 2026 as tighter supply controls supported higher prices.
The country’s biggest light rare earth producer, China Northern Rare Earth (SSE: 600111), reported net profit attributable to shareholders of 3.65 billion yuan (US$547.2 million), up 136.6% from a year earlier, according to its third-quarter results.
China Rare Earth Resources and Technology (SZSE: 000831), the main listed arm of China Rare Earth Group, posted net profit attributable to shareholders of 408.1 million yuan (US$61.2 million) for the same period, up 112.4%.
“Supply-side reforms have helped support prices by improving industry discipline,” Citi analyst Anna Wang told Reuters .
Government efforts
The earnings gains show how Beijing’s efforts to curb oversupply and consolidate production are benefiting domestic producers. Export restrictions have also become a bargaining tool in trade talks with the United States.
Prices for neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide, used in permanent magnets, have risen 62% since China introduced rare earth export controls in April 2025, to 719,000 yuan (US$107,800) per tonne, according to Shanghai Metals Market data cited by Reuters .
China allocated its first batch of 2024 mining and smelting-separation quotas to China Northern Rare Earth and China Rare Earth Group, the parent of the Shenzhen-listed company.
Rules introduced in July 2025 explicitly brought the smelting and separation of imported rare earth ore under production quotas. They also require producers to report monthly and annual quota use and enter product-flow information in a tracking system each month.
Both listed producers are on track to exceed analysts’ full-year profit estimates, Reuters reported Nov. 16.
China’s long game
China has long used production quotas and industry consolidation to manage rare earth supply.
Rare earths are used in permanent magnets and defence equipment. The sector’s price swings have squeezed producers’ profits.
China’s export controls cover selected medium and heavy rare earths and magnets containing them. NdPr oxide is outside the April 2025 restrictions.
The United States already has commercial rare earth production. MP Materials (NYSE: MP) produced 1,018 tonnes of NdPr oxide in the third quarter, up 41% from a year earlier, and said saleable magnet deliveries to General Motors would begin in the fourth quarter.

Exus Renewables North America, an independent owner, developer, and operator of utility-scale renewable energy and energy storage projects, has announced the closing of $345 million in senior secured holding company financing led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The financing will support construction costs and the development of new projects across Exus’ growing U.S. portfolio of wind, solar and battery storage assets.
The financing announced November 12 builds on an active year for Exus , including the closing of a $400 million senior secured corporate credit facility in December and approximately $356 million in project-level construction financing for its Highland North and Cambria wind projects in Pennsylvania in July . With more than 800 MW operating or under construction and a total portfolio exceeding 6 GW, Exus continues to advance its project pipeline amid rising U.S. electricity demand.
“We have projects moving forward and a deep pipeline behind them, and this financing lets us keep that momentum going,” said Jim Spencer, president and CEO of Exus Renewables North America. “The support from Goldman Sachs Alternatives reflects confidence in our team and our projects, and gives us the flexibility to keep building and bring new generation online where it’s needed.”
“Exus has established a strong platform for developing and operating utility-scale renewable energy projects,” said Vikas Agrawal, managing director and co-head of Energy Transition Climate Credit at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. “We’re pleased to support its continued investment in new energy infrastructure as electricity demand grows across the United States.”
PEI Global Partners served as financial advisor to Exus on the transaction. Latham & Watkins LLP served as legal counsel to Exus, while Vinson & Elkins LLP served as legal counsel to Goldman Sachs Alternatives.

source_document.body:
Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.
The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
Two different reporting buckets
Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service , where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:
August, Austin: drove into a large water-filled pothole in a parking lot at 5 mph, with a safety monitor on board.
September, Austin: stopped at a parking lot exit when a car backing out of a spot hit its right side.
September, Austin: stopped in traffic and rear-ended by a pickup truck.
September, Austin: drove over a raised concrete edge of a parking lot, across the sidewalk, and down a curb at up to 3 mph, with a rider on board.
Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.
The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”
There are four of them, all in September 2026:
Report | City | Road | Speed | Hit | Injury
13781-16881 | Philadelphia, PA | Highway | 53 mph | Passenger car | Unknown
13781-16964 | Austin, TX | Highway | 5 mph | SUV | Minor, hospitalized
13781-16524 | Lehi, UT | Intersection | 11 mph | SUV | Minor, not hospitalized
13781-16583 | Tampa, FL | Highway | 0 mph (stopped) | Passenger car | Property damage
Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.
The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.
Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania , and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.
Two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.
Robotaxi crashes are minor because Robotaxi is slow
Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.
Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.
Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month , Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.
The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.
The same software crashes at speed when it’s allowed to go fast
Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.
In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.
Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:
A Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida.
A Model Y at 74 mph hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California.
A Model X at 39 mph hit a pole and flipped in Naples.
Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.
The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.
Electrek’s Take
The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.
What the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.
To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.
But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

A view of the area surrounding the former Panguna copper-gold mine in Papua New Guinea. Credit: Rio Tinto.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Rio Tinto (LSE: RIO; NYSE: RIO; ASX: RIO) has pledged $250 million (C$356 million) to address environmental and human-rights impacts from the former Panguna copper-gold mine in Bougainville, Papua New Guinea, a decade after relinquishing its stake in the operator.
The contribution will be paid over coming years into a fund agreed with Bougainville Copper (ASX: BOC), the autonomous regional government and community leaders. Its governance and spending priorities still require consultation, the parties said Monday .
“Today marks a very important step on that journey,” community leader and lead complainant Theonila Roka-Matbob said in the joint announcement.
The commitment follows years of pressure from communities living with mine waste and unsafe infrastructure after production stopped in 1989. It moves the response beyond assessing damage towards financing remedies, although the announcement does not establish that the contribution will cover all outstanding work.
Rio shares fell 1.6% to $81.60 Monday morning in New York, valuing the company at about $142 billion (C$203 billion). The stock has ranged between $68.70 and $112.58 over the past year.
Continuing dangers
An independent investigation published in December 2024 identified unstable mine structures, contaminated river areas and flooding that threatened homes, food gardens and access to drinking water.
The Australian Human Rights Law Centre, which represented affected communities, said the investigation documented continuing dangers to lives and livelihoods. Environmental consultancy Tetra Tech Coffey conducted the two-year assessment after Rio agreed in 2021 to fund the work in response to a community complaint. The investigation made 24 recommendations and identified questions requiring further study, including possible health effects, the law centre said.
The risks extend beyond the former pit. Waste carried through the Jaba-Kawerong river system has affected downstream communities, while damaged infrastructure and flood-prone crossings have made access to services more difficult.
River work
The new fund will support work in river and delta areas and social programs across affected communities. Existing projects include bridge construction, hazardous-material removal at Loloho port and water and sanitation improvements. Those commitments are separate from decisions about redeveloping the mine and port, which rest with Bougainville’s government and people, the parties said.
Panguna operated from 1972 until an uprising and civil war forced its closure in 1989. Rio held a controlling interest in Bougainville Copper until 2016, when it transferred its shares to the Bougainville and Papua New Guinea governments without payment.
The long gap between closure and the current funding agreement shows how mining’s environmental and community impacts can remain unresolved long after production ends and ownership changes.
“There is still much work ahead,” Bougainville Copper CEO Sir Mel Togolo said.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is proposing road improvements, wharf rehabilitation and replacement public berths at Port Newark as part of its $10.3 billion capital and operating budget for 2027. The spending plan also includes $21 million for maintenance dredging to keep the port’s commercial shipping channels navigable.
The investments would support a port complex projected to handle 9 million twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, in 2027. The Port of New York and New Jersey is the East Coast’s busiest container port.
The proposed capital budget introduced at the bistate agency’s recent meeting would advance key components of the Port Street Corridor Improvement project, an ongoing effort to modernize the road network serving Port Newark. The work would build on the opening of the Corbin Street Ramp, which the agency identified as a major milestone in the corridor project during 2026.
On the waterfront, the plan calls for wharf rehabilitation to continue at multiple facilities and construction to begin on replacement public berths at Port Newark. These projects address the infrastructure used to accommodate vessels and support cargo handling, complementing the road improvements on the landside of the port.
Separately, the proposed operating budget includes $21 million for maintenance dredging of the commercial shipping channels serving the port. That allocation places upkeep of existing maritime access alongside longer-term improvements to roads and waterfront structures.
“The Port Authority has a responsibility to invest in the future while taking care of the infrastructure that keeps it moving today,” Chairman Kevin O’Toole said in outlining the agency’s investment and maintenance priorities.
Across all Port Authority facilities, the proposed budget includes $4 billion in annual capital spending, $4.5 billion in operating expenses, $1.7 billion for debt service and $100 million in deferred expenses. The wider program also funds airport, passenger rail, bus and other transportation infrastructure.
The 2027 spending plan remains subject to public input and final board action. Commissioners are scheduled to meet December 17 for a vote.
Why it matters: The proposed investments address three connected parts of port operations: Channels that provide vessel access, berths and wharves that support waterfront activity, and roads that connect terminals at the busiest East Coast gateway.

Amazon has its first deal with a union in North America, but it came from a top-down process in a Canadian province, rather than traditional collective bargaining.
The Amazon view of what happened for its workers at a Delta, British Columbia fulfillment center, a Vancouver suburb, was stark.
The contract for a group of workers was “imposed…without a single employee vote ever being counted, and despite a pending effort by some of those same employees to decertify the union purporting to represent them,” Amazon’s J. Ofori Agboka, Vice President, People Experience and Technology, said in an Amazon blog posting.
Meanwhile, the Unifor union, in its statement on what occurred, celebrated that its workers had “won” the first contract between a union and the e-commerce giant in North America.
The Unifor union was formed more than ten years ago through the merger of the Canadian Auto Workers and the Communications, Energy and Paperworkers Union of Canada. It describes itself as Canada’s largest private sector union.
Three-year deal for the unprecedented development
Regardless of what view of the contract one accepts, what happened in B.C. is notable because it means that Amazon, for the next three years barring some legal reversal, will be operating a facility under the terms of a collective bargaining agreement, a first for North America.
There is a Teamsters-affiliated union at a Staten Island warehouse, voted in by a grassroots organizing campaign in 2022 (before tying up with the Teamsters). But the company has refused to bargain with the unit, a dispute that has landed in federal court.
Other efforts to unionize Amazon facilities have come up short. The most notable was in Bessemer, Alabama.
Efforts to unionize the company’s Direct Service Providers that actually deliver parcels have recently been conducted by card check, with none of the DSPs recognizing the efforts (except one in California that saw its contract with Amazon yanked ). Although those DSP workers are not Amazon employees, they have sought to have the National Labor Relations Board declare that Amazon is a joint employer with the DSPs.
Union view of the process…
The union says in the headline of its prepared statement announcing the deal that it had “won” the contract. That statement then lays out the process that got it there.
“The B.C. Labour Relations Board certified Unifor Local 114 as the workers’ union in July 2025 after finding Amazon hired extra staff to frustrate the workers’ organizing drive and ran a lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign,” Unifor said in the statement.
That was followed by a board decision in August that ordered binding arbitration, “finding Amazon’s conduct had affected the parties’ ability to reach an agreement,” the union said.
The contract between the two parties–both the union and the company make reference to it as an “agreement,” although it was not agreed to in the traditional sense–is a three-year pact, ending in November 2029.
…is different from Amazon’s
The Agboka blog post recapped the process that began in 2024 in far more detail than what Unifor says about the months of back and forth.
Amazon’s Agboka says the union told Unifor it had “gathered enough support” among workers at the facility, dubbed YVR2, to hold a vote on unionization. But Agboka said an officer of the province’s Labor Relations Board disagreed with the claim of support, but “the Board ordered a vote anyway.”
An election took place soon after that. But Agboka said the results of that vote were not revealed.
According to the Agboka blog post, a Board decision in July 2025 certified Unifor as the representative of the workers. “We disagreed, believing that our employees’ voices should be heard, so we filed an appeal,” Agboka said in the blog. “The Board-ordered representation stood, and the process continued to move without a single employee vote counted.”
A decertification vote afterward, according to Agboka, also had results that were never disclosed. A legal action by workers opposed to the union has not moved forward in the B.C. Supreme Court, Amazon said.
But concurrently, Agboka said, “The Board ordered Amazon and the union to go through mediation, but we didn’t reach an agreement. So, the Board ordered an arbitrator to make a final decision on what the contract should be.”
The arbitrator’s finding is in the contract that Unifor celebrated in the announcement last week.
Some details revealed; union cites status quo
According to the union, wage increases in the contract will bring hourly rates for the workers in Delta to $CA29 per hour by the end of the three years.
There also are “enhanced severance protections” of up to 18 weeks, and an additional week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service, the union said.
A spokesman for Amazon described other aspects of the contract in an email to FreightWaves.
He said the wage increases would be zero in the first year, 3.25% in October 2027 and 3.5% a year later.
What the spokesman also disclosed was a long list of things that are not covered in the contract, with the status quo holding. Among the highlights: no change in the status of temporary and seasonal workers; no change in measurement of attendance; no right to transfer to another warehouse and no change in health benefits.
Amazon’s plan to fight the decision, noted in the Agboka blog posting, was vague. “We’ll keep challenging decisions that we believe break from long-standing precedent, keep asking for our associates’ decertification ballots to be counted, and take our concerns all the way to the Supreme Court if necessary,” he said.

source_document.body:

Lambda NVIDIA Quantum CPO Cover
For SC26, NVIDIA and Lambda discussed their first production co-packaged optics (CPO) cluster. The industry has worked to move CPO from the lab to production for decades. Many in the industry will tell you it is a few years out, but Lambda has already deployed it in production in a cluster with over 10,000 GPUs.
NVIDIA and Lambda Disclose First Production Co-Packaged Optics Cluster
We covered NVIDIA’s co-packaged optics extensively during the company’s Hot Chips 2025 presentation . NVIDIA’s first version of the packaging is in its Quantum-X switching product, while Spectrum-X will be an updated second-generation part.
NVIDIA Co Packaged Optics With Silicon Photonics At Hot Chips 2025
NVIDIA is using an array of 18 pluggable light sources on the front of the chassis, as shown in the photos above, to generate light en route to the switch package’s optical modules. Those light sources are pluggable, meaning they can be serviced, which was one of the key inhibitors to CPO in switches when the light source was integrated. Light sources tend to be the parts that fail in pluggable optics, so making them serviceable was an important innovation. Likewise, on the switch package side, making the connections at least somewhat serviceable helps with deployment.
NVIDIA Co Packaged Optics With Silicon Photonics At Hot Chips 2025
Downstream, NVIDIA’s Quantum-X CPO switch pictured above has 144 MPO/MTP ports, each at 800Gbps. Something interesting is that with only 18 light sources, instead of 144x 800Gbps optical modules (or 72x dual 800G modules), there are actually fewer light sources that can fail than in a traditional switch, and it becomes easier to cool them compared to having a larger array of individual pluggable modules.
Final Words
One of the biggest benefits of the deployment is that by moving the optics to the switch package rather than the front-panel pluggables, numerous high-speed copper links do not need to drive signaling over relatively long distances from the switch chip to the front cages. As a result, CPO can significantly lower power consumption so that more GPUs can fit in the same footprint. After all, in a power-limited environment, ultimately the more power that can be used for GPUs directly impacts the revenue that can be generated per Watt of power available to the cluster.
Patrick Quebec City Canada November 2026 in a Yellow STH Tour Filming Shirt
Lambda and NVIDIA may have a short on the cluster up, but let me be clear: it exists and is running today, putting NVIDIA at the forefront of deploying CPO. I think it is actually just being announced this week as part of SC26. As a fun aside, I was at OCP Summit 2026 a few weeks ago when I heard during another vendor’s keynote that CPO was still years away from deployment. It turns out it is already deployed. We no longer have to ask if or when CPO will finally be deployed. The big question now is what the adoption curve will be.

Asante Gold employees at a mine in Ghana. Credit: Asante Gold.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Asante Gold (TSXV: ASE; GSE: ASG) is examining whether an expanded open pit at the Bibiani mine in Ghana could defer underground development spending, as the miner works to recover from operating setbacks that forced it to withdraw this year’s guidance. The stock plunged for a second straight day.
Drilling in the Bridge area between the Main Pit and the adjacent Cut 5 pit cut 60 metres at 3.13 grams gold per tonne from 103 metres depth. Another hole cut 6 metres at 62.48 grams from 136 metres, Asante said Monday .
“Alongside the remaining drilling and test work, we are now prioritizing how best to mine this mineralization,” chief development officer Glenn Baldwin said.
The results offer a possible route to postpone spending scheduled for 2027–28, although revised economics are still being assessed. Moving material from an underground plan into a larger open pit would change how Asante accesses the deposit; it would not by itself resolve the mine’s current production problems.
Asante shares, which had dropped 34% in Toronto Friday due to the profit warning, plunged a further 45% Monday morning to 23¢ to leave the company with a $210 million (US$143 million) valuation. They have lost 87% of their value since Jan. 1.
Guidance withdrawn
Asante on Friday withdrew its 2026 production and cost forecasts , citing contractor-equipment shortages, weaker plant recoveries, power interruptions and slower resettlement at Bibiani. A second contractor is clearing waste from a January pit-wall failure, with work targeted for completion in early December and renewed ore access in the first quarter.
Group output was 48,517 gold-equivalent oz. in the third quarter, at all-in sustaining costs of $4,860 per oz., Asante said. Its realized gold price averaged $4,178 per oz. over the period.
The withdrawn August forecast had envisaged 275,000–300,000 oz. of annual production at all-in sustaining costs of $3,200–$3,600 per ounce. At the time, the company said it had already deferred or cancelled about $50 million of planned capital expenditure.
Mine plan review
The Bridge drilling forms part of an 8,000-metre program intended to improve confidence in mineralization between existing pits. Asante wants to upgrade inferred resources and test whether material assigned to underground extraction can be incorporated into a revised open-pit design.
Bibiani lies about 80 km southwest of Kumasi. The operation is one of Asante’s two producing mines in Ghana, alongside Chirano.
A broader operating turnaround plan is expected in January 2027, setting out corrective measures, milestones and capital needs, acting CEO Campbell Baird said in Friday’s results.
“We continue to make progress in resetting the business, although there is still considerable work ahead of us,” Baird said. Print

Volkswagen ID. Polo orders lead to delivery delays
The new ID. Polo is “an affordable friend for everyday life,” as Volkswagen’s chief designer Andreas Mindt calls it.
After opening orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April, starting at 33,795 euros ($37,000), Volkswagen made good on its promise, launching the lower-priced, smaller-battery model in July.
The VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.
According to the latest update from German automotive news outlet Edison Media , that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.
Volkswagen ID. Polo (Source: Volkswagen)
“We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.
The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.
As a result, the company is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI (Source: Volkswagen)
The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.
Demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

Police in Ontario, Canada, recovered 96 stolen vehicles worth approximately C$4.5 million (US$3.1 million) during an international trafficking investigation. The operation targeted a network suspected of moving luxury SUVs, pickup trucks and other automobiles overseas . Peel Regional Police announced 12 arrests and 231 criminal charges Monday, Nov. 16. Two additional suspects remain wanted in connection with the case.
The investigation, known as Project Cadetta, began in March after detectives identified a suspicious warehouse in Brampton, Ontario . Authorities discovered the facility served as a staging location for automobiles destined for international markets. Investigators traced stolen property through several locations across the Greater Toronto Area. The operation eventually uncovered a network connecting local thefts with overseas shipping arrangements .
Detectives determined that suspects targeted residential driveways, parking lots and dealerships throughout the region. Some automobiles carried altered vehicle identification numbers, commonly known as VINs. Investigators followed the movement of stolen property through holding facilities before export preparations began. Police executed search warrants during the investigation, leading to arrests and the recovery of stolen vehicles.
How stolen vehicles entered international shipping networks
The suspects allegedly concealed automobiles inside shipping containers destined primarily for West Africa. Investigators identified Montreal and Halifax as potential departure ports for the overseas shipments. Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich described a criminal supply chain connecting local vehicle thieves with international exporters. He warned that stolen vehicles from Mississauga and Brampton often reach container ships within days. Investigators targeted “every link of that criminal supply chain,” including individuals arranging exports to other countries.
The Canada Border Services Agency assisted investigators with intelligence and examinations of suspicious shipments. Trishann Pascal, the agency’s acting Greater Toronto regional director general, highlighted “targeted container examinations and referrals.” Those efforts helped authorities identify automobiles moving through the international transportation network. Police have not identified the receiving countries or individual shipping companies involved. Milinovich also reported that approximately 75% of stolen vehicles intercepted for export at Montreal’s port originate in Ontario.
Investigators identified five individuals suspected of organizing the operation. Brampton resident Stanley Udeh, 46, faces charges alongside four Toronto residents. Authorities named Odewale Abraham, Tosin Oyebade, Oluyemi Sodade and Oluwaseyi Bameke among the accused. Their cases remain before the courts, and no convictions have resulted from these accusations.
Peel Regional Police identified 12 people charged in Project Cadetta, including five suspected organizers of an international stolen-vehicle trafficking operation. (Photo: Peel Regional Police)
Seven additional adults face criminal charges connected to the investigation. The official charge sheet includes offenses involving possession of property obtained by crime and trafficking in stolen goods. Abraham faces 48 counts, while Udeh faces two forgery accusations. Toronto resident Olushola Oke, 42, faces 38 separate charges involving suspected criminal activity.
Two suspects remain wanted as investigation continues
Authorities also issued warrants for Steven Gyamfi, 32, and a 16-year-old suspect. Nine accused individuals received future court dates following their arrests. Three others attended bail hearings before obtaining release. Police expect additional charges as detectives continue examining the trafficking operation.
Peel Regional Police released images identifying Steven Gyamfi, 32, and a 16-year-old suspect wanted in connection with Project Cadetta. (Photo: Peel Regional Police)
Peel Regional Police reported vehicle thefts across Peel Region declined more than 50% from the region’s 2023 peak. Milinovich reported an additional 11.6% reduction in Peel Region as of Nov. 16. Its Commercial Auto Crime Bureau led Project Cadetta with assistance from the Canada Border Services Agency. Provincial funding through Ontario’s Preventing Auto Theft Grant Program supports local enforcement efforts.
Authorities have not identified commercial trucking companies, freight brokers or shipping lines knowingly participating in the suspected operation. Police provided no specific dates for upcoming court proceedings. Anyone with information can contact Peel Regional Police’s Commercial Auto Crime Bureau at 905-453-2121, ext. 3410.
Why it matters
The investigation demonstrates how stolen automobiles can move through warehouses and international shipping networks. Freight professionals face potential exposure when criminals introduce illicit property into legitimate transportation channels.
CFCO
Stolen cargo can move through multiple hands and reach international markets within days, making recovery increasingly difficult. Once a shipment leaves the country, investigators face additional challenges tracing its movement and identifying those responsible. The Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) program teaches transportation professionals to verify companies, individuals and shipment details before releasing freight. In my view, recognizing suspicious activity before cargo changes hands offers a far better opportunity to prevent theft than attempting recovery after it reaches an overseas destination.

By: Staff Writer November 16, 2026
CleanTech Lithium (AIM: CTL) faces another delay in obtaining a lithium operating contract for its Laguna Verde project in Chile after the country’s Comptroller General returned the approval decree to the government with observations, the company said Monday.
The regulator sent the decree back to the Ministry of Economy and Mining on Nov. 13, CleanTech said. Although it has received no official communication, the company understands the decree has not been rejected and the ministry is working to address the observations. It provided no revised approval timetable.
“We are encouraged by the continued engagement and efforts of the Chilean authorities to progress the approval, even over this weekend,” CEO Ignacio Mehech said in the release.
The delay leaves the operating contract unresolved for a proposed $748-million (C$1.07-billion) development designed to produce 15,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate annually over 25 years. CleanTech plans to use direct lithium extraction at Laguna Verde, about 275 km by road from Copiapó in northern Chile.
CleanTech shares closed 5.3% stronger at 6p in London on Monday, valuing the company at about £21.9 million. The gain followed a 19% decline on Friday.
Former government
The company agreed contract terms with Chilean authorities in March, under former president Gabriel Boric’s administration, and initially expected ratification in the second quarter. The proposed 40-year Special Lithium Operating Contract, known by its Spanish acronym CEOL, covers 153 sq. km and would span exploration, evaluation, construction, production and closure.
CleanTech has not disclosed the nature of the regulator’s observations. The contract’s ratification would not replace the project’s other permitting, technical work and financing requirements.
A prefeasibility study released in March, with a correction issued in April, estimated the capital cost including contingency and outlined probable reserves of 378,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent at an average lithium concentration of 186 mg per litre.
An estimate issued in November 2025 put measured and indicated resources at 835,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent at 178 mg lithium per litre, plus inferred resources of 1.065 million tonnes at 167 mg per litre.
That resource estimate includes a surface-lake component, while the proposed operating contract excludes the lake surface. CleanTech said in March that the estimate might require revision to reflect the final contract boundary.

Image: Vattenfall
Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.
Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council ( GWEC ), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
More wind means fewer batteries
Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.
That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.
In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.
The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.
“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember.
By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.
What happens when it’s cloudy and still?
The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.
That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.
Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.
New coal and gas doesn’t make financial sense
The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.
Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.
In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.
Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.
For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.
Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

source_document.body:
There’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.
But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?
Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.
The motorcycle fatality statistics are ugly
In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.
But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.
Around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS . In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.
Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.
Then there are the bikes themselves.
Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.
That’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.
But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.
To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.
The LiveWire S4 Honcho has built huge excitement despite its largely urban approach
We give inexperienced riders access to absurd performance
One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.
Someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.
And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.
That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.
For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire .
Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.
But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.
The next generation of electric motorcycles looks different
Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho .
This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.
It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving .
And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.
That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.
Battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.
So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.
Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.
Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.
Electric scooters that offer light motorcycle-level performance are also growing in popularity
Then there’s the e-bike generation
This is where I think things get even more interesting.
For decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly quickly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.
But now we’re raising an entirely new generation on electric two-wheelers.
Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.
Today’s e-moto teens are tomorrow’s electric motorcycle riders. And that’s a good thing.
A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.
That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.
There’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.
That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.
The rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.
Electric motorcycles like those from LAND Moto are inherently easier to ride and control for new riders
Electric doesn’t automatically mean safer
To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.
They’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them .
If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.
And electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.
There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.
But that’s not really my argument.
My argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more important, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.
I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.
But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.
A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.
Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.
What excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Canadian Copper (CSE: CCI) has raised $9.8 million (US$6.8 million) through warrant exercises, lifting its treasury above $24 million as it advances a plan to feed its Murray Brook deposit into the idled Caribou processing plant in New Brunswick.
The company is targeting late January for a feasibility study of the combined development, according to a statement Monday . It also identifies up to $32 million in remaining stream financing and $50 million in project debt, bringing potential funding to about $106 million.
The cash “further strengthens our balance sheet and positions Canadian Copper to advance several development milestones over the coming months,” CEO Simon Quick said.
The proposed development pairs an undeveloped deposit with existing processing infrastructure, potentially reducing the cost of returning metal production to the Bathurst mining camp. Caribou’s 3,000-tonne-per-day plant lies about 10 km east of Murray Brook and includes crushing, grinding and flotation equipment, grid power and water supply.
Canadian Copper shares dropped 8.5% to 48¢ Monday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about $103 million. Canadian Securities Exchange data show a 52-week range of 29¢ to 82¢.
Funding conditions
The $106-million figure combines cash with potential future financing. Access to construction payments under the precious-metals stream depends on milestones including permits, board approval, execution contracts and sufficient funding to complete the development, according to the financing terms disclosed in April.
Under that agreement, OR Royalties (TSX: OR; NYSE: OR) is entitled to 20% of payable gold and silver from the combined operation, with ongoing purchase payments equivalent to 20% of spot prices. The stream exchanges part of future precious-metal revenue for capital upfront. OR Royalties was previously known as Osisko Gold Royalties, having changed its name last year.
Canadian Copper received $12.5 million when the stream and an associated equity investment closed in July. The company then identified about $31.5 million of additional stream payments for construction, providing the basis for the rounded remaining amount cited Monday.
Study and permits

Brixton Metal's camp at the Langis project on the shore of Lake Temiskaming in northeast Ontario. Credit: Brixton Metals.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Brixton Metals (TSXV: BBB) has drilled its highest silver grade yet at the Langis project in Ontario, finding shallow veins in a new target area as it works towards an initial resource estimate. The stock surged.
Hole LM-26-477 cut 3 metres at 14,559 grams silver per tonne from 68.5 metres depth, including 0.3 metre at 142,770 grams, Brixton said Monday . A follow-up hole cut 5 metres at 704 grams from 67 metres.
The narrower interval was “the highest-grade silver intercept ever drilled on the project,” chairman and CEO Gary Thompson said.
Brixton shares surged 10% to 55¢ Monday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about $53 million (US$37 million). The stock has ranged between 45¢ and $1.45 over the past year.
Short intervals
The results add a shallow target to a property with a long production history, but the short intervals require care: true widths are unknown, and further drilling must establish continuity. The headline assay measures silver concentration in a small section of core, rather than the size of a deposit.
Langis lies about 500 km north of Toronto in the Cobalt district, within the traditional territory of Timiskaming First Nation. Highway 65 crosses the property, which has access to power and rail infrastructure.
The new Shaft 4 target contains silver in the upper part of a conglomerate rock unit. Most known mineralization lies near its lower contact, giving Brixton another horizon to test beneath the shallow veins.
July intercept
The discovery follows a wider intersection announced in July at Shaft 6 Southeast, where hole LM-26-377 cut 20 metres at 5,015 grams silver per tonne from 165 metres depth. That result included 14 metres at 7,150 grams.
The former Langis mine produced more than 10.4 million oz. of silver and about 358,000 lb. of cobalt, according to Brixton. Its workings extend roughly 150 metres below surface and are flooded.
Although historical production establishes the district’s mining pedigree, it doesn’t establish a current resource for Brixton’s new targets.
Exploration funding
Brixton closed the final portion of a $7.16-million (US$5.02-million) flow-through share financing Friday. The proceeds are intended mainly for exploration and drilling at Langis and the Thorn copper-gold project in British Columbia.
The financing involved about 10.2 million shares across three closings. Flow-through financing allows qualifying exploration expenditures to be passed through to investors for tax purposes, directing the money towards exploration rather than general corporate spending. Print

SEVOS studied 20 roles a freight company wanted to outsource. It came back with an answer most vendors would not give: three of them were unnecessary.
The client pushed back. SEVOS put floaters in those three seats and gave them no work, to show the workflow would hold. Three weeks later the client had the proof and three fewer roles to pay for.
“That also builds trust with the customer where they trusted us with more,” said Jay Singh, SEVOS’ chief operating officer.
Jay Singh, who ran a trucking company before co-founding SEVOS with Michael McLary, said the Atlanta-based company soft-launched last year and has grown to 225 people. Earlier this year, before the official launch, SEVOS brought in Tom Carr to lead the commercial side of the business as SVP of Customer Solutions. The company made its public launch official at FreightWaves’ F3: Future of Freight Festival in Chattanooga.
Singh’s point is simple. Plenty of freight companies have been told to adopt AI. Many are doing it without a clear picture of what to automate, by when, or what it will cost. SEVOS fills the role first, documents it, and measures it. Only then does it decide what software should take over.
“You have to bring the customer along for the journey,” he said.
SEVOS Spends 30 Days Learning Each Role
The first week is spent identifying the roles. The second is spent collecting and studying the client’s standard operating procedures. By day 30 a SEVOS team member is working the seat. Each role gets KPIs and coaching tools before anything is automated. In sales development work SEVOS already handles, callers use AI-assisted scripts and get real-time AI tutoring.
Which Freight Tasks Get Automated First
Track-and-trace paperwork is the first place automation lands. Collecting proofs of delivery and bills of lading, scanning them, and moving them into accounting is repetitive and rule-bound.
“That stuff is getting automated really, really fast, and it should,” Singh said.
Carrier negotiation, relationship building, and sales development stay with people. The work around those conversations can still be automated. A proposal that follows a sales call, for example, can be generated and sent in real time instead of waiting until the end of the day.
Clients choose the technology, including whether to use open-source or closed-source models and whether to host them on their own servers. Over time SEVOS wants customers to pay a fee for each transaction rather than a headcount.
Clients See the Work as It Happens
SEVOS Insights, the company’s reporting tool, shows the client every action a team member takes. It can also connect to the client’s own system, such as Tableau, so productivity is visible person by person.
Coverage Across Shifts and Time Zones
SEVOS runs teams in India, Serbia, and Atlanta, all working on Eastern time. The India team is based in Chandigarh. Serbia fills the hours between India’s shift and the U.S. morning. The model supports day-shift work, including sales development, as well as coverage outside normal business hours. Customers decide which seats and which hours to staff based on the work, not a fixed starting point.
The team works in English, Spanish, Serbian, Punjabi, Hindi, and Haryanvi. That matters in carrier sales and with newly authorized trucking companies.
AI agents are the last layer. Put them on top of a follow-the-sun team and the client is covered across the spectrum.
Singh’s own job description is short. “225 people report to me,” he said. “However, I report to every single one of my customers.”
